title: Lost in a mall that never happened

probes.question: About what share of participants reported remembering the false event in the formal follow-up?
True or false: the false event in the study was getting lost in a shopping mall.

image.alt: A tall glass-roofed shopping centre interior seen from an escalator.

panels.text: Can people remember something that never happened? Elizabeth Loftus and her student Jim Coan set out to test it.
Coan gave his brother a booklet of four childhood stories to remember over six days. One was false: getting lost in a shopping mall at around age five and being rescued by an elderly person.
His brother invented extra details, and at the end could not tell which story was false.

In a formal follow-up with 24 participants, Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell found that about 25% reported remembering the false event. Loftus suggests it forms as the suggested event gets built into existing memories of going to the mall.
